Promotions likely leak margin; price sensitivity still has to be tested

The client asked: how price-sensitive is each product, how much do features and displays add beyond the price cut, and which products can take a price increase without losing profit?

The data cannot yet answer the first and third questions reliably. Every method gives a different price sensitivity, and the econometric model gives the wrong sign. The demand forecast is accurate only because one input (VISITS) nearly duplicates sales. No cost data exists, so profit cannot be calculated. What the data does show is heavy discounting that probably loses money. The recommendation is promotion discipline now and store-level price tests next.

About this report: sources, evidence labels and corrections applied

Project: 05-pricing-simulator | Date: 16 Nov 2026 | Author: report-writer Sources: every number cites its file and section. Short forms: EXP = reports/exploration/findings.md; DD = reports/exploration/data_dictionary.md; HTM = reports/exploration/handoff_to_modeling.md; MC = reports/modeling/model_card.md; TUN = reports/modeling/tuning.md; HR = reports/ml_handoff_report.md; FU = reports/ml_followups.md (R1/R2 = round, Q = question); MEMO = reports/executive_growth_strategy.md; DIA = reports/agent_dialogue.md; NBR = reports/notebook_review.md.

Evidence labels. measured = counted directly from the data. modeled = output of a statistical model; an association, not proof of cause. external = from a cited web source. assumed = an analyst's estimate or arithmetic on other figures.

Corrections applied throughout. The statistician corrected several handoff numbers after the fact (FU R1, "CORRECTIONS"). This report uses the corrected values only:

  • Revenue is $9.56M a year, not $1.49B. The $1.49B was an arithmetic error.
  • VISITS counts shopping trips that included the product. It is an outcome, not store traffic.
  • The exploration price slopes (−1.44, −1.16, −0.34, −0.38) could not be reproduced.
  • The cleaned file holds 13,693 duplicate rows.
  • Exploration finding F2 ("Bag Snacks and Cereal rarely discounted") is wrong.
  • Exploration finding F4 ("~20 of 55 products make 80% of revenue") is corrected to 25 of 55.

Part AThe answer in plain language

The answer, numbers, actions and uncertainty

The question the client asked

A grocery chain sets one price and promotion rule per aisle. Its category managers asked three things (problem_description.md):

  1. How price-sensitive is each product?
  2. How much do weekly-ad features and in-store displays add beyond the price cut?
  3. Which products can take a price increase without losing profit?

The answer

The data cannot yet answer the first and third questions reliably. Every method gives a different price sensitivity, and the econometric model gives the wrong sign. The demand forecast is accurate, but only because one input (VISITS) nearly duplicates the sales it predicts. No cost data exists, so profit cannot be calculated. What the data does show is that discounting is heavy and probably loses money. About 37% of revenue sells on discount, and no category's average discount week recovers its markdown at an assumed 30% margin. The recommendation is promotion discipline now and store-level price tests next, not price cuts.

What is uncertain

  • All margin and break-even figures rest on assumed 30% and 40% margins; no cost or vendor-funding data exists.
  • True price sensitivity per product is unknown; only randomised store tests can measure it.
  • The data is from 2009–2011 and the external benchmarks are from 2016–2026, so gaps are directional only.

B3. How the model was built: accurate on unseen weeks, but for the wrong reason

What it predicts. Weekly units for one product in one store (MC "What the model predicts").

How it was tested. The last 26 weeks (88,751 rows) were held out [kept unseen until the end]. The first 130 weeks (449,684 rows) trained the model (HR §8). Models were compared with 5-fold expanding-window cross-validation [CV: train on earlier weeks, score on the next block, repeat five times] (MC "How it was tested").

What was compared (modeling/tables/final_model_comparison.csv; RMSE_log [typical error on the log scale; 0.10 is roughly ±10% in units]; modeled).

LightGBM, XGBoost, CatBoost and Random Forest are tree models [many small decision rules added together]. Ridge and OLS are regressions [straight-line formulas]; fixed effects [a separate baseline for each store and product] absorb level differences. Chart: 08_model_comparison.png.

How it was tuned. Optuna [software that tries many settings and learns which work] ran trials [one full test of one set of settings] for the two best families (TUN).

The history charts show most gains came in the first 10–15 trials; later trials moved the error by about 0.001 (modeling/charts/optuna_lgb_history.png, optuna_xgb_history.png). Tuning improved LightGBM from 0.1063 to 0.1043 (modeled; table above).

Why LightGBM won. It had the lowest CV error, narrowly ahead of tuned XGBoost (MC "Selected model"). Ridge was kept separately only to estimate price sensitivity.

B6. The strategy: promotion discipline first, then store-randomised price tests

LeverWhat changesAnnual impact on these 4 categories

Five pilots (MEMO §5). All randomise by store, stratify by tier and size, and read results by difference-in-differences [change in test stores minus change in control stores]. Effect ranges and MDEs [minimum detectable effect: the smallest change the test can see] are assumed.

B7. The agent dialogue: 14 questions in two rounds reshaped the strategy

The growth-strategy partner sent questions to the statistician by direct message. Questions are verbatim from DIA. Answers are quoted from FU (key lines; full tables in FU). No question was declined and none remains open (DIA).

Round 1 (8 questions plus 1 optional)
Round 1 · Q1Memo §1, §2, §3
Strategy partner asked"Total revenue. decile_revenue.csv and category_segment_detail.csv sum SPEND to about $30.2M over 156 weeks. Handoff §2 and §6b state $1.49B total / $801M Cereal "annualised". Which is correct? Please give total SPEND and annual SPEND (total/3) by category."
Statistician answered"Total $28.69M over 156 weeks = $9.56M/year." "Your figures are right; the report is wrong."
Revenue corrected; levers re-sized; corrections box added
Round 1 · Q2Memo §3.3, §3.4, A2, B1
Strategy partner asked"VISITS definition. data_dictionary.md defines VISITS as "shopping trips including this product" (an outcome, r=0.99 with UNITS), not store traffic as handoff §5 states. Please confirm, and confirm the §6e counterfactual held VISITS fixed at observed values when price was cut 10%. Also give median UNITS/VISITS overall."
Statistician answered"Confirmed: VISITS = trips including the product (outcome). corr(UNITS, VISITS) = 0.987. Median UNITS/VISITS = 1.038." "the +0.8% to +3.2% figures are a lower bound on a real price response, not a measure of it."
Simulator frozen for price decisions; counterfactual relabelled a lower bound
Round 1 · Q3Memo §3.3, §1
Strategy partner asked"Exploration slopes (−1.44, −1.16, −0.34, −0.38): are they each fit across one point per UPC (~10–15 points per chart 01)? Give n and SE for each slope; reconcile with hypotheses.md H3 and findings.md F1."
Statistician answered"I could not reproduce chart 01's slopes" "The exploration outputs are mutually inconsistent." "Treat the category ranking "Bag Snacks and Pizza most price-sensitive" as NOT established."
Slopes labelled not reproducible; thesis withdrawn; Pilot 2 moved to Cereal
Round 1 · Q4Memo §1, §2, §3.2
Strategy partner asked"By category: % of store-weeks with PRICE < BASE_PRICE; % with FEATURE=1; % with DISPLAY=1; mean discount depth; % of SPEND sold in discounted weeks."
Statistician answered"all four categories are discounted in 23-29% of rows. Chart 02/finding F2 ... is a median artifact"
~37% discount share and ~$1.0M markdown derived; F2 exposed
Round 1 · Q5Memo §3.2, Pilot 4
Strategy partner asked"By category × promo type (None, TPR only, Display only, Feature only, Feature+Display): row count, median UNITS per store-week, median UPV."
Statistician answered"Units lift (2-4x) is far larger than UPV lift (0-15%), meaning promos mostly raise trips including the product, not units per trip."
Pilot 4 (display without discount) added
Round 1 · Q6Memo §3.4, B1, risks
Strategy partner asked"Promo lift ratio (promoted / non-promoted median units) by store segment within each category."
Statistician answered"Value stores are NOT consistently the highest." "It was a product-mix artifact."
Value-store targeting withdrawn
Round 1 · Q7Memo §3.3
Strategy partner asked"For rows with PRICE > BASE_PRICE (~2%): count by category, and median units in those weeks vs median units at PRICE = BASE_PRICE for the same UPC-store pairs."
Statistician answered"total 6,264 = 1.2% of rows (not ~2%)." "Units are HIGHER in price-increase weeks in all four categories."
Confirms prices follow demand; test before rollout
Round 1 · Q8Memo §2, Lever 3, Pilot 5, B5
Strategy partner asked"Revenue share of private-label UPCs by category; mean shelf price of PL vs national-brand UPCs within each category."
Statistician answeredPL share: Bag Snacks 41.6%, Cereal 13.9%, Pizza 24.9%, Oral 17.2%
Lever 3, Pilot 5 and B5 added
Round 1 · QoptMemo §5
Strategy partner asked"week-to-week CV for pilot sizing"
Statistician answered"median Bag 0.46, Cereal 0.36, Pizza 0.55, Oral 0.55"
Pilot MDE calculations
Round 2 (6 questions)
Round 2 · Q1Memo §5
Strategy partner asked"Number of stores by segment (Mainstream / Upscale / Value), and number of distinct stores selling each category."
Statistician answered"77 stores: Mainstream 43, Upscale 15, Value 19. Every store carries all four categories"
38 vs 39 store arms; tier stratification
Round 2 · Q2Memo §3.2, Lever 1, Pilots 1, 3
Strategy partner asked"By category: median SPEND per store-UPC-week in discounted vs undiscounted rows (same store-UPC pairs). Revenue lift ratio."
Statistician answeredRatio of medians: Bag 1.15, Cereal 1.55, Pizza 2.29, Oral 1.23. "this is not a price effect."
Break-even table added
Round 2 · Q3Memo §3.2
Strategy partner asked"Post-promotion dip. By category: median units in the first undiscounted week after a discounted week vs undiscounted weeks ≥3 weeks away from any discount."
Statistician answered"No post-promotion dip is visible in medians"
Main risk is markdown waste, not pull-forward
Round 2 · Q4Memo §3.1, B4
Strategy partner asked"By category: median discounted weeks per store-UPC per year; median length of consecutive discount runs."
Statistician answeredWeeks a year: Bag 11.0, Cereal 11.6, Pizza 16.2, Oral 13.8; run length 2–4 weeks
Informs holdout design
Round 2 · Q5Memo §3.3, Pilot 2
Strategy partner asked"By category: median BASE_PRICE changes per UPC over 156 weeks; share that are chain-wide (same week, ≥90% of stores)."
Statistician answered"Base price is changing often and mostly store by store, not chain-wide" (2.6%–9.0% of change events chain-wide)
Store-level price tests judged operationally normal
Round 2 · Q6Memo §3.1
Strategy partner asked"Number of UPCs making up 80% of SPEND, out of 55 total."
Statistician answered"25 of 55 UPCs (45%) account for 80% of total SPEND."
F4 corrected; Pilot 2 targets top 25

Remaining gaps:

  • Exploration: no alternatives named for the lift-ratio chart; no formal null hypothesis [the "no effect" statement a test tries to reject] for H1, H2, H4–H6; discount direction missing in the data dictionary.
  • Modeling: three diagnostic cells have no captured output (decile lift, permutation, SHAP plots); diagnostics and Ridge fit lack explanatory notes; no "Finding" notes after residual, decile, threshold, permutation and SHAP results; XGBoost min_child_weight missing from the tuning search-space table; features.md lacks formula, expected direction and example row.

The review stopped at its one-fix-round limit (NBR).

Part DAppendix

D1. Glossary

Every underlined term in the report opens its entry in the glossary panel.

TermPlain meaning
Base priceThe regular everyday shelf price before any temporary discount.
Basket haloExtra items a shopper buys on a trip because a promoted item drew them in.
Bayesian optimisationA search that uses past trial results to choose the next settings to try.
Break-even liftThe unit increase a discount needs to earn the same margin dollars: m ÷ (m − d).
CatBoost, XGBoost, LightGBMThree tree-based forecasting programs that add many small decision rules together.
CI (confidence interval)The range likely to contain the true value; here 95% likely.
colsample_bytreeThe share of inputs each tree is allowed to see; lower values reduce over-fitting.
CollinearityTwo inputs carrying almost the same information.
Correlation (r)How closely two numbers move together, from −1 to 1.
CounterfactualA "what if" run: change one input and re-score the model.
Cross-validation (CV)Testing a model several times on blocks of data it did not train on.
Cumulative gainThe share of all units captured by the top-ranked rows.
DecileOne tenth of the rows, ranked by predicted units.
Difference-in-differencesChange in test stores minus change in control stores over the same period.
DisplayAn in-store secondary placement such as an end-cap.
DriftA model's accuracy slipping as conditions change.
ElasticityThe % change in units for a 1% change in price. −1.5 means a 1% price rise cuts units 1.5%.
Expanding windowEach test fold trains on all weeks before it.
FeatureInclusion in the retailer's weekly circular ad.
Fixed effects (FE)A separate baseline for each store and product.
Gross marginRevenue minus cost of goods.
Held-out test setData kept unseen until the end to judge the final model.
Holdout / control storesStores that do not get the change, used for comparison.
HyperparameterA setting chosen before training, such as number of trees.
IV / 2SLS / instrumentA two-step method using a price driver unrelated to demand, such as a cost change, to isolate cause.
LeakageWhen an input contains the answer the model predicts, as VISITS does here.
Learning rateHow large a step each new tree takes.
LiftHow much higher a group's result is than the average or baseline.
Log / log-log slopeLogarithm turns % changes into straight-line distances; the slope of log units on log price.
MAPEMean absolute percentage error: the average miss as a % of actual units.
Mann-Whitney UA test comparing two groups by rank rather than average.
MarkdownDollars given away by selling below the base price.
max_depth, num_leaves, min_child_samples, min_child_weightLimits on how detailed each tree may become.
MDE (minimum detectable effect)The smallest change a test can reliably see.
MedianThe middle value when sorted.
n_estimatorsNumber of trees in the model.
Net marginProfit after all costs as a share of sales.
Null hypothesisThe "no effect" statement a test tries to reject.
OLSOrdinary least squares: a straight-line regression.
OptunaSoftware that tries many hyperparameter settings and learns which work.
Outcome variableA number produced by the thing being predicted, not a cause of it.
p-valueThe chance of seeing a result this large if there were no real effect.
Permutation importanceHow much error rises when one input is shuffled.
Pruned trialAn Optuna trial stopped early because it was not promising.
Pull-forwardShoppers buying ahead during a deal, lowering later sales.
R²Share of variation in the outcome a model explains.
Random ForestMany decision trees averaged together.
Rank-biserial rEffect size for Mann-Whitney: 0 no effect, 1 full separation.
reg_alpha, reg_lambdaPenalties that shrink weak inputs to reduce over-fitting.
RegressionA formula linking an outcome to inputs.
RidgeA regression with a penalty that keeps coefficients small.
RMSE / RMSE_logRoot mean squared error; on the log scale, 0.11 is roughly ±12% in units.
SE (standard error)The typical uncertainty of an estimate.
SHAPShapley additive explanations: each input's average contribution to a prediction.
Spearman ρA rank-based correlation.
Store brand (private label, PL)The retailer's own-label products.
Store tierThe chain's store segment: Mainstream, Upscale or Value.
StratifyBalance test and control groups on key traits such as tier and size.
subsampleShare of rows each tree trains on.
ThresholdA cut-off on predicted units used to flag rows.
TPRTemporary price reduction without a feature ad or display.
Trade spend / vendor fundingMoney manufacturers pay retailers to fund promotions.
TrialOne test of one set of model settings.
UPCUniversal product code: one product at one pack size.
UpliftThe extra effect of an action compared with no action.
UPVUnits per visit: units ÷ trips that included the product.
VISITSShopping trips that included the product that week.

Share of rows each tree trains on.
Threshold
A cut-off on predicted units used to flag rows.
TPR
Temporary price reduction without a feature ad or display.
Trade spend / vendor funding
Money manufacturers pay retailers to fund promotions.
Trial
One test of one set of model settings.
UPC
Universal product code: one product at one pack size.
Uplift
The extra effect of an action compared with no action.
UPV
Units per visit: units ÷ trips that included the product.
VISITS
Shopping trips that included the product that week.
